stem: A client taking felodipine extended-release says, "I drink grapefruit juice every morning." Which teaching by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Take felodipine later in the day and keep grapefruit juice at breakfast, because separating them by several hours prevents a clinically important interaction.
options.B: Continue the usual grapefruit juice and monitor blood pressure at home, because the interaction becomes important mainly after symptoms such as dizziness occur.
options.C: Avoid routinely combining grapefruit juice with felodipine and discuss the regular grapefruit use with the prescriber or pharmacist because it can markedly increase felodipine exposure and effects.
options.D: Reduce grapefruit juice to a smaller serving and continue felodipine unchanged, because a reduced serving reliably prevents a clinically important increase in felodipine exposure.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling states that felodipine is metabolized by CYP3A4 and that grapefruit juice can increase felodipine plasma exposure; coadministration produced more than a twofold increase in both AUC and Cmax. Increased concentrations can intensify pharmacologic effects such as lower blood pressure and increased heart rate, so grapefruit use should not simply be continued without review. A incorrectly assumes that several hours of separation reliably prevents the interaction. B waits for symptoms despite a known interaction. D assumes that reducing the serving size reliably eliminates the interaction, which is not supported by the label.
educational_objective: Recognize grapefruit juice as a clinically important CYP3A4-mediated interaction with felodipine and teach the client to avoid routine coadministration and clarify regular grapefruit use with the prescribing team.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_locator: Drug Interactions > CYP3A4 Inhibitors: felodipine is metabolized by CYP3A4; CYP3A4 inhibitors including grapefruit juice can increase felodipine plasma concentrations and may increase effects such as lower blood pressure and increased heart rate. Grapefruit Juice interaction: coadministration produced more than a twofold increase in felodipine AUC and Cmax.
source_claim_supported: Grapefruit juice can more than double felodipine exposure and may intensify its blood-pressure and heart-rate effects through CYP3A4 inhibition.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–41: identify actual and potential medication interactions, provide medication education, evaluate client response to medications, and intervene when adverse effects or interactions are identified.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — felodipine and grapefruit interaction
correction_summary: Rebuilt all distractors to remove absolute-word cueing and replaced them with realistic but unsupported interaction-management strategies involving dose timing, symptom-triggered monitoring, and smaller grapefruit servings.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Calcium-channel blocker therapy — grapefruit interaction with felodipine
audit_findings.stem: PASS — identifies ongoing grapefruit exposure in a client taking felodipine extended-release and asks one medication-teaching decision.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — spacing medications can be appropriate for some interactions, but the label does not support several-hour separation as a reliable solution for grapefruit-mediated CYP3A4 inhibition.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — home blood-pressure monitoring can be useful, but known interaction risk should be addressed before waiting for symptoms.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS — directly reflects the labeled grapefruit interaction and appropriately routes regular grapefruit use for medication-plan review; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — reducing serving size does not provide a label-supported guarantee that the interaction is prevented.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — C is the only option that acknowledges the documented interaction without relying on an unsupported workaround.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A, B, and D each preserve grapefruit exposure through a strategy not established as protective by the prescribing information.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — no option contains an absolute-word pattern that uniquely signals correctness, and all responses are clinically plausible teaching choices.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes medication interactions and client education.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether timing separation or reduced grapefruit quantity could be accepted; the label documents a marked grapefruit interaction without providing either workaround as reliable, leaving C uniquely safest and most accurate.
